question: A replacement processor fits the same general size as the old CPU. What must still be verified before installation?
options: Only the processor's brand and physical dimensions
The motherboard socket, chipset and firmware support the exact CPU
Only the CPU's advertised clock speed
Only that the power supply has spare connectors
explanation: Physical appearance does not establish compatibility. The socket, board support list and required firmware must support that CPU model.

lesson.title: CPU compatibility
lesson.meaning: A socket is the processor's physical and electrical interface; board support also depends on its design and firmware.
lesson.example: A board accepts a CPU only after a supported firmware update. Check the vendor list before purchasing.
lesson.remember: Check the exact CPU support list, not just the brand.

question: Which memory is designed to keep frequently used instructions and data close to the CPU for fast access?
options: CPU cache
System RAM used for all active applications
Nonvolatile SSD storage used for saved files
Virtual memory pages stored on a drive
explanation: Cache reduces the delay of obtaining frequently needed information. It is small, fast memory associated with the processor, not long-term file storage.

lesson.title: CPU cache
lesson.meaning: Think of cache as a small set of frequently used items kept within immediate reach.
lesson.example: A processor accesses cached data instead of fetching every item from slower main memory.
lesson.remember: Cache = small and fast; RAM = larger working memory; storage = persistent files.

question: What is a principal purpose of error-correcting code (ECC) memory in a supported system?
options: Encrypt all stored files automatically
Replace the need for redundant storage
Make unsupported RAM work in any motherboard
Detect and correct supported memory errors
explanation: ECC adds information that enables supported memory-error detection and correction. The platform must support ECC; it is not a substitute for backup.

lesson.title: ECC memory
lesson.meaning: ECC improves memory reliability by handling certain bit errors.
lesson.example: A supported server platform uses ECC to reduce the effect of correctable memory faults.
lesson.remember: ECC concerns memory errors, not permanent file storage.

question: Two laptops have USB-C ports. Why might only one support an external display through that port?
options: All USB-C ports must support identical optional features
A cable adapter always adds missing display support
Connector shape does not guarantee the same protocols or capabilities
The operating system alone guarantees video capability
explanation: USB-C describes the connector. Video output and charging capabilities depend on the implementation and supported modes.

lesson.title: USB-C capabilities
lesson.meaning: A matching plug shape does not mean every optional function is present.
lesson.example: Check the laptop and dock specifications for supported display output before buying a cable.
lesson.remember: Connector type and supported features are separate checks.

question: Which slot is commonly used for a desktop's discrete graphics card?
options: A DIMM slot with enough physical clearance
A compatible PCI Express x16 slot
A SATA connector configured in firmware
The CPU socket used for processor installation
explanation: A discrete graphics card commonly connects through PCIe. Memory modules and processors use different sockets and cannot substitute for the expansion interface.

lesson.title: Expansion slots
lesson.meaning: PCIe expansion lets compatible devices communicate with the system.
lesson.example: A GPU is fitted into the appropriate PCIe slot, with any required additional power connected.
lesson.remember: GPU expansion commonly uses PCIe; RAM goes in DIMM slots.

question: Why should a technician not force a DDR4 module into a DDR5 motherboard memory slot?
options: The generations have different keying and electrical requirements
The modules differ only in advertised speed
The operating system can adapt the slot electrically
The notch can be removed without affecting compatibility
explanation: Different DDR generations are not interchangeable merely because both are memory. Mechanical keying helps prevent incompatible installation.

lesson.title: DDR compatibility
lesson.meaning: The notch is a compatibility feature, not an obstacle to overcome.
lesson.example: A module's notch does not align. Stop and verify the supported generation.
lesson.remember: Never force memory; match the supported DDR generation.

question: A compatible motherboard has four RAM slots. What is the best source for choosing the slots for a two-module dual-channel configuration?
options: Always the two slots closest to the CPU on every board
Always two adjacent slots regardless of channel labels
Any two slots necessarily enable the intended mode
The motherboard manual's recommended population order
explanation: Recommended slot placement depends on the board design. The manual identifies the correct pair for the intended configuration.

lesson.title: Memory channels
lesson.meaning: Memory channels depend on the controller and correct module placement.
lesson.example: The manual recommends A2 and B2; use that pair rather than assuming adjacent slots are correct.
lesson.remember: Use the board's population diagram; slot layout is not universal.

question: When selecting a PSU for a new graphics-card upgrade, what should be considered?
options: Only the graphics card's slot length
Only the PSU's maximum advertised wattage, ignoring connectors
System power needs, suitable connectors and the vendor's requirements
Only the old PSU's age
explanation: A PSU must support the full system and provide appropriate connections. A single wattage figure without checking compatibility is insufficient.

lesson.title: PSU capacity
lesson.meaning: The power supply is selected for the system it must power.
lesson.example: A GPU requires dedicated power connectors and higher capacity; check both before upgrading.
lesson.remember: Capacity, connectors, quality and compatibility all matter.

question: Which part distinguishes a typical mechanical hard drive from an SSD?
options: Nonvolatile storage of user files
Spinning magnetic platters and moving read/write heads
A logical partition table
A controller for storage commands
explanation: A mechanical HDD uses moving components to access magnetic storage. SSDs store data electronically without those storage mechanisms.

lesson.title: Mechanical storage
lesson.meaning: Mechanical storage moves; solid-state storage does not.
lesson.example: An HDD makes unusual clicking sounds and read errors appear. Protect data and investigate the drive.
lesson.remember: HDD = mechanical magnetic storage; SSD = solid-state storage.

question: Where is motherboard firmware normally stored so it remains available without main power?
options: Nonvolatile firmware memory on the motherboard
Only in volatile RAM refreshed while powered
Only on the operating-system partition
Only in the battery itself
explanation: Firmware must remain available when the system is off so it can start the machine. Nonvolatile storage retains its contents without normal system power.

lesson.title: Firmware storage
lesson.meaning: Startup instructions need persistent storage.
lesson.example: A PC can enter firmware setup before any operating system is installed.
lesson.remember: Firmware persistence is different from RAM's temporary working data.

question: What should be done if a CPU does not seat easily in its supported socket?
options: Increase pressure until the retention bracket closes
Rotate the processor according to its printed brand text only
Treat every CPU from that vendor as socket-compatible
Check the orientation and alignment marks without forcing it
explanation: Correct orientation is essential. Forcing a CPU can damage pins or contacts even when the model is otherwise compatible.

lesson.title: CPU alignment
lesson.meaning: Alignment marks show how a processor must be positioned.
lesson.example: The triangle markers do not align; reposition the CPU before closing the retention mechanism.
lesson.remember: Match the orientation and follow the socket instructions.

question: A new CPU cooler has a protective film over its contact surface. What must happen before fitting it?
options: Leave the film to prevent electrical contact
Compensate for the film with extra thermal paste
Remove the film according to the cooler instructions
Increase fan speed instead of removing the film
explanation: Protective film is packaging, not a thermal interface. Leaving it in place can obstruct heat transfer.

lesson.title: Cooler preparation
lesson.meaning: The cooler needs the intended contact with the CPU through the specified thermal interface.
lesson.example: A new build overheats immediately; inspection finds protective film under the cooler.
lesson.remember: Check packaging film, seating and thermal-compound instructions.

question: For a case using a separate snap-in motherboard I/O shield, when is it normally fitted?
options: After the motherboard is fully secured over it
Before mounting the motherboard in the case
After all rear cables are attached
Only after the operating system is installed
explanation: A separate shield fits the case opening behind the board's ports. Installing it first avoids having to remove the board again; integrated shields differ.

lesson.title: Rear I/O shield
lesson.meaning: The I/O shield frames the rear connectors; it is not an internal electrical cable.
lesson.example: Check whether the board uses an integrated shield or a separate piece before mounting.
lesson.remember: Follow the case/board design; a separate shield normally goes in first.

question: After assembly, the case power button does nothing. The PSU and main power connections check out. What should be checked next?
options: The power-switch lead on the correct front-panel header pins
The storage drive's partition scheme
The monitor's selected video input
The operating system's startup-app list
explanation: The case switch signals the motherboard through its front-panel connection. Incorrect placement can prevent the button from triggering startup.

lesson.title: Front-panel wiring
lesson.meaning: The front-panel switch is a control connection, distinct from the PSU's main power plug.
lesson.example: Use the motherboard pinout to verify the case power-switch connector.
lesson.remember: Use the header diagram; do not guess pin positions.

question: A newly installed GPU has power sockets specified by its manufacturer. What is the appropriate action?
options: Assume the PCIe slot always supplies all required power
Use any visually similar CPU connector without checking
Use an unapproved adapter regardless of PSU capability
Connect the required compatible PSU leads before operation
explanation: Some GPUs need power in addition to what the slot provides. Use the specified compatible connectors and follow the hardware instructions.

lesson.title: Expansion-card power
lesson.meaning: The PCIe slot and supplementary leads may both contribute power.
lesson.example: A GPU displays a missing-power warning; check its specified connections.
lesson.remember: Match the device's required power connectors; never force plugs.

question: A screw falls beneath the motherboard during assembly. What should the technician do before applying power?
options: Leave it if the computer passes one startup test
Power on first to see whether a short occurs
Retrieve it and check for other loose conductive parts
Assume a screw cannot contact exposed conductors
explanation: A loose metal object can bridge conductors and cause a short. Remove it safely before powering the system.

lesson.title: Loose hardware
lesson.meaning: Conductive debris can turn a physical assembly error into an electrical fault.
lesson.example: Account for dropped screws before closing and powering a case.
lesson.remember: No loose conductive hardware inside a powered system.

question: Why should motherboard screws be tightened only as directed rather than excessively?
options: Extra force improves the board's electrical grounding indefinitely
Excessive force can damage the board or mounting points
Screw pressure sets the CPU's operating frequency
The board must bend slightly to ensure connector seating
explanation: Mounting should secure the board without unnecessary stress. Overtightening can damage components, threads or the circuit board.

lesson.title: Correct mounting
lesson.meaning: Mechanical security does not require excessive force.
lesson.example: Tighten evenly with the correct tool and follow the manufacturer's guidance.
lesson.remember: Secure, not forced; avoid stressing the board.

question: A technician replaces one modular PSU with another brand. Which cable practice is safest?
options: Use cables specifically approved for the new PSU model
Reuse old modular cables whenever the shells fit
Mix cables according to the number of pins only
Assume all PSU-side wiring is standardized across models
explanation: PSU-side modular pinouts are not universally interchangeable. A fitting connector does not establish electrical compatibility.

lesson.title: Modular PSU cables
lesson.meaning: The removable cable's PSU end must match that PSU's wiring.
lesson.example: Use the new PSU's supplied or explicitly compatible cables rather than assuming old ones are safe.
lesson.remember: Modular PSU cables are not universally interchangeable.

question: Where should a standard CPU cooler's fan normally connect when the board manual specifies CPU_FAN?
options: The front-panel power-switch pins
The clear-CMOS jumper
An unverified header chosen only because it has the same pin count
The motherboard's designated CPU_FAN header
explanation: The designated header powers and monitors the fan according to the board design. Wrong placement can cause monitoring warnings or incorrect control.

lesson.title: CPU-fan header
lesson.meaning: Fan headers are functional control and power connections.
lesson.example: The cooler spins but the firmware reports no CPU fan; verify the instructed header and sensor setup.
lesson.remember: Use the designated cooler header and the manufacturer's instructions.

question: Which check is appropriate before a newly assembled PC is powered for the first time?
options: Apply power before checking for loose screws
Assume seated connectors need no inspection
Verify connections, component seating and clear fan movement
Install the operating system before verifying cooler mounting
explanation: A final physical inspection catches preventable wiring, seating and obstruction problems before power is applied.

lesson.title: Final assembly check
lesson.meaning: A short pre-power checklist prevents avoidable faults.
lesson.example: Check RAM latches, power leads, cooler mounting and loose objects before startup.
lesson.remember: Inspect before applying power, then test systematically.

question: A PC keeps starting the old installed OS instead of the prepared installer USB. What firmware setting is relevant?
options: The installed OS's startup-app order
Boot-device selection or order
The storage volume's display name
The browser's default download location
explanation: Firmware chooses a startup device before the OS runs. Selecting the correct supported media is necessary to launch its installer.

lesson.title: Boot order
lesson.meaning: Boot order determines which available startup target is attempted.
lesson.example: Use the one-time boot menu to choose the installer rather than altering unrelated Windows settings.
lesson.remember: Boot selection happens before the installed OS loads.

question: Before updating motherboard firmware, which preparation is most important?
options: Verify the exact model, correct firmware and reliable power
Use a similar board's firmware if the version number is higher
Perform the update without checking power stability
Assume the newest file is compatible with every board revision
explanation: Wrong firmware or an interrupted update can leave the system unable to start. Follow the exact vendor procedure and compatibility requirements.

lesson.title: Firmware update preparation
lesson.meaning: Firmware is foundational startup software, so its update needs careful matching.
lesson.example: Check the board revision and approved update method before flashing.
lesson.remember: Exact model, correct update, stable power, vendor procedure.

question: What is a common role of a Trusted Platform Module (TPM)?
options: Provide additional general-purpose RAM
Supply temporary power during an outage
Replace the need to manage encryption recovery keys
Support secure cryptographic key operations and platform security
explanation: A TPM supports security functions involving protected keys and platform integrity. It is not a general-purpose performance upgrade.

lesson.title: TPM
lesson.meaning: Security hardware can help protect key material used by other security features.
lesson.example: A device-encryption deployment checks TPM requirements and recovery-key arrangements.
lesson.remember: TPM supports security; it does not replace backups or recovery planning.

question: A compatible hypervisor reports that hardware virtualization is disabled. Where might a technician need to enable it?
options: The VM's desktop background settings
The printer-sharing settings
The system's UEFI/BIOS virtualization setting
The guest's file-system volume label
explanation: Supported CPUs may have virtualization features controlled by firmware. Verify platform support and the appropriate setting.

lesson.title: Hardware virtualization
lesson.meaning: Capability and configuration are separate: a supported feature may still be disabled.
lesson.example: Enable the documented virtualization option, then restart as required and retest.
lesson.remember: Check both hardware support and firmware enablement.

question: A healthy RAID 5 array loses one drive. What property can allow it to continue operating in a degraded state?
options: Every disk contains a complete independent copy
Distributed parity permits reconstruction of one failed drive's data
The array has no redundant information
Striping alone recreates missing data with no parity
explanation: RAID 5 combines striping with parity and can tolerate one drive failure in the usual configuration. Additional failures during degraded operation can cause loss.

lesson.title: RAID 5
lesson.meaning: Parity stores information used to reconstruct missing data; it is not a full mirror on every disk.
lesson.example: Replace the failed disk and rebuild according to the controller procedure while maintaining independent backups.
lesson.remember: RAID 5: parity, at least three disks, one-disk fault tolerance.

question: What is the usual minimum number of drives for a RAID 10 array combining mirrored pairs with striping?
options: Four
Two, because one mirrored pair also supplies the required striped pairs
Three, because RAID 10 is identical to RAID 5
One, because virtual volumes do not need physical drives
explanation: RAID 10 stripes across mirrored pairs. At least two pairs are required, giving the standard four-drive minimum.

lesson.title: RAID 10
lesson.meaning: It combines mirroring for redundancy with striping across the pairs.
lesson.example: A technician plans two mirrored pairs before creating a striped set across them.
lesson.remember: RAID 10 = stripes across mirrors; standard minimum four drives.

question: Which device can supply temporary battery power during an outage so a PC can shut down gracefully?
options: A basic surge-only power strip
A passive outlet adapter with no battery
An external PSU extension cable
Uninterruptible power supply (UPS)
explanation: A UPS includes stored energy and power-support functions. A simple surge protector does not provide sustained battery power during an outage.

lesson.title: UPS
lesson.meaning: A UPS buys time; it is not an unlimited electricity source.
lesson.example: Configure supported shutdown behavior so work can be saved before the UPS battery is exhausted.
lesson.remember: UPS = temporary power during interruption.

question: Why is a surge-protected strip alone insufficient for an extended power outage?
options: Surge protection always replaces the computer's PSU
It automatically creates an orderly OS shutdown
Surge suppression does not supply backup battery energy
It converts every outage into a harmless voltage spike
explanation: Protecting against voltage spikes differs from supplying electricity when mains power disappears.

lesson.title: Surge protection
lesson.meaning: Different power problems require different protection functions.
lesson.example: Choose suitable backup power when continuity through a short outage is needed.
lesson.remember: Surge protection and battery backup are different functions.

question: Why should a firmware setup password not be treated as equivalent to full-disk encryption?
options: Setup passwords and disk encryption always protect identical data
Restricting setup access does not itself encrypt stored files
Any firmware password encrypts all removable storage
Disk encryption only changes firmware-menu access
explanation: An access-control setting and data encryption protect different things. Storage protection requires appropriate encryption and recovery arrangements.

lesson.title: Firmware password scope
lesson.meaning: A password prompt is not evidence that the underlying disk contents are encrypted.
lesson.example: A removed unencrypted drive may expose data despite a firmware setup password.
lesson.remember: Access restriction is not the same as encryption at rest.

question: A firmware change prevents startup. What is the best source for an approved recovery procedure?
options: The exact motherboard or system manufacturer's documentation
A procedure for any board using the same CPU brand
A generic instruction to short pins while powered
An OS installation guide that ignores firmware recovery
explanation: Recovery methods vary by model. Guessing jumper positions or update procedures can make the problem worse.

lesson.title: Firmware recovery
lesson.meaning: Hardware recovery needs model-specific instructions.
lesson.example: Consult the documented recovery or reset method and its effect on settings before acting.
lesson.remember: Use exact-model recovery guidance, not visual similarity.

question: Why is changing one variable at a time useful during diagnosis?
options: It guarantees that the first proposed cause is correct
It eliminates the need for final verification
It makes documentation unnecessary
It helps identify which change affects the symptom
explanation: When several things change together, it becomes difficult to identify the cause of an improvement or a new fault.

lesson.title: Controlled troubleshooting
lesson.meaning: A controlled test connects evidence to a specific change.
lesson.example: Replace one suspect cable, retest, and record the result before changing a second part.
lesson.remember: One controlled change → one interpretable result.

question: A PC loses network link. Replacing only its cable with a known-good equivalent restores it. What is the best interpretation?
options: The DNS service is proven to be the only possible fault
The entire network is proven healthy in every respect
The original cable or its connection is implicated by the test
The CPU is proven defective by the restored link
explanation: A known-good substitution isolates a component or connection. It is useful evidence, though final verification and documentation still matter.

lesson.title: Known-good testing
lesson.meaning: Compare a suspect component with an equivalent that works.
lesson.example: Retest with the replacement cable and record stable link operation.
lesson.remember: Use equivalent known-good parts to narrow the cause.

question: Which information is particularly useful for an intermittent shutdown?
options: Only the current desktop appearance
Time, workload, temperatures and relevant logs when it occurs
Only the installed application's icon name
Only the replacement part's purchase price
explanation: A fault that comes and goes may depend on load, environment or timing. Correlating evidence helps identify the triggering conditions.

lesson.title: Intermittent problems
lesson.meaning: Intermittent means conditions matter; capture the pattern.
lesson.example: Shutdowns happen only under heavy load and rising temperatures, directing attention to cooling and power.
lesson.remember: Record when, under what conditions, and what changed.

question: Before troubleshooting a failing drive containing important files, what is a priority?
options: Protect required data using an appropriate approved recovery/backup approach
Run a destructive reformat before considering the data
Perform repeated write-intensive tests regardless of the fault
Assume a drive that still mounts needs no recovery planning
explanation: Troubleshooting can worsen some storage faults. Protecting important data and following an appropriate recovery process comes before avoidable write-intensive or destructive actions.

lesson.title: Protecting data
lesson.meaning: A repair is not successful if it unnecessarily destroys the customer's data.
lesson.example: Escalate a physically failing drive with critical unbacked data rather than experimenting with destructive tools.
lesson.remember: Protect data before risky storage work.

question: What is an appropriate way to choose a computer-cleaning method?
options: Use household cleaning chemicals on exposed powered circuitry
Use any vacuum without considering ESD or device instructions
Choose the strongest air pressure regardless of the device
Follow the manufacturer's procedure and ESD precautions
explanation: Cleaning methods must suit electronics and the device. Inappropriate liquids, tools or static-generating methods can cause damage.

lesson.title: Dust removal
lesson.meaning: Preventive maintenance must not create a new fault.
lesson.example: Power down as instructed and use approved cleaning tools for vents and components.
lesson.remember: Use the device's approved cleaning process.

question: When using an approved air-cleaning method on a fan, what precaution may be required?
options: Force the blades to maximum speed using the air stream
Hold the fan by bending a blade
Keep the fan from overspinning as instructed and avoid damage
Ignore the manufacturer's handling precautions
explanation: Uncontrolled airflow can overspin or damage a fan. Follow the manufacturer's guidance for holding or protecting it during cleaning.

lesson.title: Fan cleaning
lesson.meaning: Cleaning airflow and normal powered operation are not the same condition.
lesson.example: Clean accumulated dust using the recommended distance and fan-handling precautions.
lesson.remember: Clean fans safely; do not use compressed air to race them.

question: A desktop is completely unresponsive. Which is an appropriate initial check?
options: Reinstall Windows before checking incoming power
Verify the outlet, power cable and PSU switch
Replace the motherboard before checking the outlet
Reset application preferences before verifying PSU input
explanation: A system cannot start without incoming power. Checking the external supply path is a simple relevant first step.

lesson.title: No-power diagnosis
lesson.meaning: Start with basic prerequisites before costly replacements.
lesson.example: A switched-off PSU rocker explains a no-power condition without an internal component failure.
lesson.remember: No power: verify the external power path first.

question: A PC starts overheating immediately after its cooler was removed and refitted. What should be checked first?
options: Cooler seating, fan connection and thermal interface
The user's unrelated email configuration
The monitor's display color profile
The printer's selected paper size
explanation: The recent change is strong diagnostic evidence. An improperly mounted cooler or fan connection can explain the new temperature fault.

lesson.title: After-service fault
lesson.meaning: Ask what changed just before the symptom started.
lesson.example: Inspection finds the fan lead disconnected after cooler servicing.
lesson.remember: Correlate the fault with the most recent relevant change.

question: Random crashes suggest a possible RAM fault. Which next step provides relevant evidence?
options: Assume every random crash proves a failed RAM module
Reinstall the OS without testing the suspected memory
Replace the display cable as a definitive RAM test
Run an appropriate supported memory diagnostic
explanation: A memory diagnostic can help test the suspected subsystem. Crashes alone are not proof of defective RAM.

lesson.title: Memory testing
lesson.meaning: Symptoms suggest a theory; testing supplies evidence.
lesson.example: Use a supported memory test and assess results alongside seating and compatibility checks.
lesson.remember: Suspected RAM faults should be tested, not assumed.

question: A technician notices a burning smell and visible damage while a computer is operating. What is the appropriate response?
options: Continue powered stress testing to reproduce more damage
Open the connected PSU to inspect its internals
Stop use, isolate power safely and follow the incident/service procedure
Keep using the system if an application still responds
explanation: Continuing operation may worsen an electrical fault. Safe isolation and qualified assessment take priority over routine diagnosis.

lesson.title: Stop-work condition
lesson.meaning: Some symptoms require stopping work rather than continuing ordinary tests.
lesson.example: Power is safely isolated and the damaged unit is routed for approved assessment.
lesson.remember: Smoke, burning or electrical damage: stop and follow safe procedures.

question: Which transport protocol provides an ordered, reliable byte stream between applications?
options: UDP
TCP
ARP
ICMP
explanation: TCP uses mechanisms including sequencing and retransmission to provide reliable ordered delivery. UDP does not provide the same transport guarantees.

lesson.title: TCP
lesson.meaning: Transport protocols provide different communication services.
lesson.example: A file-transfer application needs delivered data in order and uses TCP.
lesson.remember: TCP = reliable ordered stream; UDP = datagrams without those guarantees.

question: Which statement describes UDP at the transport layer?
options: It sends datagrams without TCP-style connection setup and delivery guarantees
It guarantees ordered delivery and retransmits every lost datagram
It inherently encrypts all application data
It uses TCP's mandatory connection establishment
explanation: UDP provides datagram transport without built-in ordered reliable delivery. Applications can implement extra behavior themselves.

lesson.title: UDP
lesson.meaning: A lightweight transport can favor timely sending over waiting for retransmissions.
lesson.example: A real-time application may tolerate some loss rather than delaying every update.
lesson.remember: UDP itself does not guarantee delivery or order.

question: Which TCP port is conventionally associated with HTTPS?
explanation: HTTPS conventionally uses TCP 443 for secure web communication. Other listed ports serve different common purposes.

lesson.title: HTTPS port
lesson.meaning: A port identifies a service endpoint, not a physical connector.
lesson.example: A firewall rule for a conventional HTTPS service allows its required TCP destination port.
lesson.remember: HTTPS commonly uses TCP 443.

question: Which service conventionally uses TCP port 22 for secure remote administration?
options: Telnet
FTP control
SSH
RDP
explanation: SSH commonly uses TCP 22 and provides encrypted remote access. A port number alone still does not prove a service's identity.

lesson.title: SSH port
lesson.meaning: Remote-management protocols differ in purpose and protection.
lesson.example: An administrator selects SSH rather than an unencrypted remote terminal protocol.
lesson.remember: SSH commonly uses TCP 22.

question: Which port is conventionally used by DNS over UDP or TCP?
explanation: Traditional DNS uses port 53 and can use UDP or TCP. Treating DNS as UDP-only overlooks supported TCP uses.

lesson.title: DNS transport
lesson.meaning: One service can use more than one transport.
lesson.example: A network must permit the DNS traffic required by its design rather than assuming every lookup uses only one transport.
lesson.remember: Traditional DNS: port 53, UDP and TCP.

question: Which UDP port pair is associated with DHCPv4 servers and clients?
options: Server 67 and client 68
Server 68 and client 67
Server 53 and client 53
Server 80 and client 443
explanation: DHCPv4 uses UDP 67 on the server side and 68 on the client side. These support configuration exchange, not name resolution.

lesson.title: DHCP ports
lesson.meaning: DHCP has distinct client and server communication roles.
lesson.example: An address-allocation capture shows DHCP messages between the client and server port pair.
lesson.remember: DHCPv4 = UDP 67/68.

question: What information does a typical Ethernet switch use to learn which port leads to a local device?
options: Only the source IP subnet mask
The destination application's user account
Only the configured DNS server address
Source MAC addresses observed in frames
explanation: A switch learns source MAC addresses on ingress ports and uses its forwarding information for destination frames.

lesson.title: Switch forwarding
lesson.meaning: MAC addresses support local Ethernet delivery.
lesson.example: After a PC sends a frame, the switch can associate its source MAC with the receiving port.
lesson.remember: Switch learning uses source MAC addresses and ingress ports.

question: What is a typical role of a wireless access point?
options: Route all networks regardless of its configured function
Assign every client's address without any DHCP service
Connect wireless clients to a network
Replace the wired network's switching function in every design
explanation: An AP provides wireless network access and typically bridges clients into the associated network. Routing and internet service may be separate functions.

lesson.title: Wireless access point
lesson.meaning: Wireless access and routing are distinct roles even when one home device combines them.
lesson.example: An office adds APs for Wi-Fi coverage while retaining its existing router.
lesson.remember: AP = wireless access; router = forwards between networks.

question: Why might fiber be selected for a link near strong electromagnetic interference?
options: Fiber always eliminates distance limitations
It carries optical signals and is not subject to EMI pickup like copper conductors
Any fiber connector works with every transceiver
Fiber automatically supplies PoE to attached devices
explanation: Fiber transmits light rather than electrical data signals in copper. Compatible optics, distance and installation requirements still apply.

lesson.title: Fiber and interference
lesson.meaning: Choose a medium for the environment, not only the connector's appearance.
lesson.example: A link near industrial equipment uses suitable fiber and optics.
lesson.remember: Fiber resists electromagnetic interference but still needs compatible equipment.

question: How many conventional usable host addresses are in an IPv4 /26 subnet?
explanation: A /26 leaves 6 host bits: 2^6 gives 64 addresses. For a conventional subnet, subtract the network and broadcast addresses to get 62 usable hosts.

lesson.title: Subnet capacity
lesson.meaning: Prefix length determines how many bits remain for hosts.
lesson.example: A segment requiring 50 host addresses fits within a conventional /26 capacity.

question: A host is 192.168.10.20/24. Which destination is in its local subnet?
explanation: With /24, the first three octets identify this network. 192.168.10.200 shares that network portion.

lesson.title: Local versus remote
lesson.meaning: Use the mask rather than guessing from one matching number.
lesson.example: The host can attempt local delivery to 192.168.10.200 without treating it as a remote subnet.
lesson.remember: For this /24, local addresses share 192.168.10.

question: Which dotted-decimal subnet mask corresponds to /26?
explanation: A /26 has 24 one-bits in the first three octets and two more in the last. Binary 11000000 is decimal 192.

lesson.title: Prefix conversion
lesson.meaning: A prefix is the count of leading network bits.
lesson.example: Convert /26 by writing 26 leading ones rather than memorizing an unrelated host count.

question: What is the broadcast address for 192.168.10.0/24?
explanation: In this /24, all host bits set to one produce .255. The .0 address is the network address.

lesson.title: Broadcast address
lesson.meaning: Broadcast and network addresses occupy distinct roles in a conventional subnet.
lesson.example: Do not assign 192.168.10.255 as an ordinary host on that /24.
lesson.remember: For 192.168.10.0/24: network .0; broadcast .255.

question: Which Windows command is intended to query DNS records during troubleshooting?
options: nslookup
ipconfig /renew
tracert
netstat -an
explanation: nslookup queries DNS, providing relevant evidence for name-resolution problems. The other commands act on processes or storage.

lesson.title: DNS testing
lesson.meaning: Test the service that matches the symptom.
lesson.example: An IP works but a name fails; query that name with nslookup and inspect the response.
lesson.remember: nslookup = DNS query tool.

question: Which Windows command helps identify the sequence of router hops toward a destination?
options: nslookup
ipconfig /all
arp -a
tracert
explanation: tracert probes the path and reports responding hops. Missing replies may reflect filtering, so output needs interpretation.

lesson.title: Route tracing
lesson.meaning: A path test differs from checking only one endpoint.
lesson.example: A technician compares where responses stop along a route, while considering ICMP filtering.
lesson.remember: tracert explores the path; ping tests echo reachability.

question: Which address is commonly used to test the local IPv4 loopback interface?
explanation: 127.0.0.1 refers to the local host through loopback. A successful loopback test does not prove the physical network works.

lesson.title: IPv4 loopback
lesson.meaning: A local networking-stack test can succeed with the cable unplugged.
lesson.example: Ping loopback while diagnosing local networking, then test the actual interface and network separately.
lesson.remember: Loopback success is not proof of external connectivity.

question: Which command requests renewal of a Windows DHCP configuration on applicable adapters?
options: ipconfig /flushdns
ipconfig /renew
ipconfig /displaydns
nslookup
explanation: /renew requests DHCP renewal; /flushdns clears cached DNS resolver entries. They address different functions.

lesson.title: DHCP renewal
lesson.meaning: An address lease and a cached name lookup are different things.
lesson.example: After fixing a DHCP connectivity issue, request renewal and inspect the resulting configuration.
lesson.remember: /renew = DHCP lease; /flushdns = resolver cache.

question: A client reaches an external service by IP but cannot resolve its hostname. What should be investigated next?
options: DNS configuration and name-resolution responses
Replace the CPU before examining DNS
Treat a successful IP test as proof that name resolution works
Change printer drivers before testing the hostname lookup
explanation: Successful IP communication narrows the issue, while failed lookup specifically points toward DNS investigation. It does not prove every network component is healthy.

lesson.title: Isolating name-resolution faults
lesson.meaning: Separate addressing/connectivity tests from name-resolution tests.
lesson.example: Use ipconfig /all and nslookup to inspect the configured DNS path.
lesson.remember: IP works, name fails: investigate DNS.

question: What does IPv4 NAT commonly do on an internet gateway?
options: Resolve every domain name without DNS
Provide guaranteed end-to-end encryption
Replace all firewall rules with authentication
Translate addresses between an internal network and another addressing domain
explanation: NAT changes address information according to a translation policy. It is not itself a replacement for a complete firewall or authentication design.

lesson.title: NAT
lesson.meaning: Private addressing and public-facing communication can use translation.
lesson.example: Several internal clients access services through a gateway's translation rules.
lesson.remember: NAT translates addresses; it does not mean all traffic is safe.

question: What does a Wi-Fi SSID primarily identify?
options: A guarantee of the AP operator's identity
A mandatory secret that cannot be copied
The wireless network's name
Proof that strong wireless encryption is enabled
explanation: An SSID labels a wireless network. The name alone does not authenticate the operator or establish encryption strength.

lesson.title: SSID
lesson.meaning: A familiar label can be copied by another transmitter.
lesson.example: Verify the intended network and its security rather than trusting a name alone.
lesson.remember: SSID = network name, not proof of trust.

question: A laptop's Wi-Fi suddenly stops after a key combination is pressed. What is a useful initial check?
options: Replace the adapter before checking whether radios are disabled
Airplane mode and wireless enable settings
Reinstall the OS before checking wireless settings
Change the network's DNS record before checking the local radio
explanation: A wireless-disable control can stop connectivity without a failed adapter. Check settings and recent actions first.

lesson.title: Airplane mode
lesson.meaning: A configuration switch can look like hardware failure.
lesson.example: Re-enable wireless if it was unintentionally disabled, then reconnect and test.
lesson.remember: Check wireless controls before replacing the adapter.

question: A laptop display is dim after a function-key press, but an image is clearly present. What should be checked first?
options: Brightness settings and the relevant function-key controls
Replace the entire display before inspecting brightness settings
Repartition the system drive before checking the control
Treat it immediately as a proven GPU failure
explanation: The timing and symptom suggest a setting change before a component replacement. Check the simple control first.

lesson.title: Brightness control
lesson.meaning: Recent changes provide diagnostic clues.
lesson.example: Restore brightness using the documented keys or display settings and retest.
lesson.remember: A dim screen may be a setting, not a failed display.

question: How should a removed laptop battery be disposed of?
options: Dispose of it in general waste regardless of local procedures
Puncture it to remove stored charge before recycling
Burn it to prevent data recovery
Through an approved battery recycling or disposal process
explanation: Batteries require appropriate handling and disposal. Burning or puncturing them can create hazards.

lesson.title: Battery disposal
lesson.meaning: Disposal is part of safe servicing, not an afterthought.
lesson.example: Use the organization's or manufacturer's approved collection route.
lesson.remember: Use approved battery disposal; do not puncture or burn.

question: Which statement normally describes hibernation?
options: It retains the session only in continually powered RAM
It is the same as an ordinary restart with no saved state
It saves session state to storage for later resume with power removed
It always keeps every component fully powered
explanation: Hibernation stores the session state on persistent storage. Sleep typically retains the session in powered memory, with platform-specific behavior.

lesson.title: Hibernate versus sleep
lesson.meaning: Different low-power states preserve work differently.
lesson.example: A user chooses supported hibernation before an extended period without external power.
lesson.remember: Hibernate saves state to storage; sleep normally relies on retained memory power.

question: Before replacing a laptop's system drive, what should be planned?
options: Only verify that the replacement has a similar label
Data backup, recovery/installation media and hardware compatibility
Replace first and consider data recovery afterward
Assume replacing the drive retains the old installed OS automatically
explanation: Replacing the system drive affects data and startup. Compatible hardware and a recovery path must be prepared.

lesson.title: Storage upgrade preparation
lesson.meaning: An upgrade includes migration and recovery, not just swapping hardware.
lesson.example: Verify required files and installation/recovery tools before removing the old drive.
lesson.remember: Protect data and plan how the new drive will boot.

question: While replacing an internal Wi-Fi card, what should guide antenna-lead handling?
options: The exact service manual's connector positions and removal method
Pull on the antenna wires instead of the connectors
Choose the lead positions randomly
Treat every internal antenna connector as mechanically identical
explanation: Small antenna connectors and leads are easily damaged. Follow the model-specific procedure and documented placement.

lesson.title: Laptop antenna leads
lesson.meaning: Serviceable parts can still have fragile connections.
lesson.example: Record lead positions and disconnect using the approved technique.
lesson.remember: Follow the manual; do not pull fragile connectors by their wires.

question: A laptop touchpad stops responding while an external mouse works. What is an appropriate initial check?
options: Replace the touchpad before examining its enable state
Repartition storage to restore pointer input
Replace all RAM because an external mouse works
Touchpad enable settings and any hardware/function-key toggle
explanation: A disabled touchpad can explain the symptom without a hardware failure. Verify controls and relevant driver/device status.

lesson.title: Touchpad controls
lesson.meaning: Use the symptom to isolate the affected input path.
lesson.example: Check whether a shortcut or setting disabled the touchpad before ordering a replacement.
lesson.remember: Check enable settings before assuming a failed touchpad.

question: Why is the exact laptop service manual useful before internal replacement?
options: All models use an identical disassembly order
Physical resemblance guarantees identical replacement parts
Disassembly order and supported parts vary by model
A model manual removes the need for ESD precautions
explanation: Compact devices use model-specific fasteners, connectors and procedures. Guessing can damage cables or the case.

lesson.title: Service documentation
lesson.meaning: A similar-looking laptop is not the same service design.
lesson.example: Check screw lengths and battery-isolation steps in the exact model guide.
lesson.remember: Exact model, approved part, documented procedure.

question: A laptop has USB-C, but a small phone charger cannot sustain it under load. What must be checked?
options: Assume every fitting USB-C charger supplies enough power
Supported charging method and adequate adapter/cable power capability
Assume any USB-C cable supports every charging capability
Change the OS theme to enable higher adapter wattage
explanation: The connector shape does not guarantee compatible charging negotiation or enough power. Verify the laptop, charger and cable specifications.

lesson.title: USB-C charging
lesson.meaning: Charging depends on supported power capabilities, not only a fitting plug.
lesson.example: Use a compatible adapter and cable meeting the laptop's required power specifications.
lesson.remember: USB-C shape alone does not establish charging compatibility or wattage.

question: Why should a replacement laptop adapter match manufacturer requirements?
options: Connector, voltage and power specifications must be compatible
Only the connector's external dimensions
Only the adapter's brand name
Only whether the adapter can turn on its indicator light
explanation: An unsuitable adapter may fail to power the laptop or cause damage. Match the documented electrical and connector requirements.

lesson.title: Power adapter compatibility
lesson.meaning: Power compatibility is a hardware requirement.
lesson.example: Select the approved compatible adapter rather than guessing from connector size.
lesson.remember: Check voltage, connector and required power capability.

question: Which printer feature prints on both sides of a sheet?
options: Collation
Color calibration
Print spooling
Duplex printing
explanation: Duplex describes two-sided output. Collation concerns page ordering and OCR concerns recognizing text.

lesson.title: Duplex printing
lesson.meaning: Printer terms refer to distinct functions.
lesson.example: Enable duplex for a two-sided report when the printer and driver support it.
lesson.remember: Duplex = both sides of the paper.

question: What does an automatic document feeder (ADF) primarily do?
options: Bond toner to the printed sheet
Sort completed printed pages into sets
Feed multiple originals for scanning or copying
Convert digital jobs into a spool queue
explanation: An ADF feeds source pages to the scanner. It is not the printer's fuser or an operating-system feature.

lesson.title: ADF
lesson.meaning: The input path for originals differs from the output printing mechanism.
lesson.example: Load a multi-page original into the ADF instead of placing every page manually on the glass.
lesson.remember: ADF = automatic feeding of originals.

question: A printer's built-in test page prints correctly, but one PC cannot print. What does this suggest?
options: The entire network path is proven healthy
The printer can produce output; investigate the client's driver, queue or connection
The printer's mechanical output is proven impossible
All printer drivers on all clients are proven correct
explanation: A local test separates physical output capability from the client's print path. Further testing is needed to isolate the client issue.

lesson.title: Standalone test page
lesson.meaning: Test at different points in the chain.
lesson.example: Compare printer-local output with jobs from the affected PC and another client.
lesson.remember: A good local test narrows the fault; it does not prove the client path works.

question: After a driver change, a printer produces unreadable characters from one PC. What should be checked?
options: Correct driver and page-description-language compatibility
The display driver, before examining the printer driver
The printer's paper size as the only possible cause
The CPU's thermal interface as the primary print-language setting
explanation: An unsuitable driver can send output the printer interprets incorrectly. Verify the exact model and supported driver.

lesson.title: Printer driver mismatch
lesson.meaning: The driver translates application output into a supported print language.
lesson.example: Install the approved compatible driver and print a test page.
lesson.remember: Correct printer model and supported driver matter.

question: One print job is stuck and later jobs do not proceed. What should be investigated?
options: The monitor's active display input
The computer's CPU power connector
The printer's cosmetic panel color
The queue and spooler using the approved troubleshooting process
explanation: A blocked queue can prevent later work despite a functioning print mechanism. Review the specific job and spooler state.

lesson.title: Stuck queue
lesson.meaning: Queue management and physical printing are separate stages.
lesson.example: Resolve the stuck job with appropriate authorization, then submit a test job.
lesson.remember: A queue blockage may affect later jobs.

question: Repeated paper jams occur after damp paper is loaded. What is an appropriate first action?
options: Apply lubricant to the paper sheets
Compensate by changing the IP subnet mask
Use suitable dry paper and inspect the approved paper path
Assume all media types and humidity conditions feed identically
explanation: Media condition and suitability affect feeding. Follow the printer's supported media and jam-clearing instructions.

lesson.title: Paper handling
lesson.meaning: Paper is a consumable with requirements, not an arbitrary sheet.
lesson.example: Replace damp stock and load the tray correctly before retesting.
lesson.remember: Check media condition, size, loading and paper path.

question: Which technology can print on heat-sensitive paper without a liquid ink cartridge?
options: Thermal-transfer printing that requires a ribbon
Direct thermal printing
Dot-matrix impact printing with an inked ribbon
Inkjet printing with liquid ink cartridges
explanation: Direct thermal printers activate heat-sensitive media. This differs from thermal-transfer ribbon printing and other methods.

lesson.title: Direct thermal printing
lesson.meaning: The required consumables depend on the print process.
lesson.example: A receipt printer uses compatible heat-sensitive paper rather than an inkjet cartridge.
lesson.remember: Direct thermal = heat-sensitive media.

question: What does increasing a scanner's selected DPI generally increase?
options: Sampling detail and often file size
The scanner's physical page-feed capacity
The printer's available toner quantity
The network's permitted host count
explanation: More samples per inch can preserve more detail but often produce larger files. Choose a setting suitable for the original and purpose.

lesson.title: Scan resolution
lesson.meaning: Higher resolution has storage and processing tradeoffs.
lesson.example: A high-detail image scan may need more DPI than a simple document archive.
lesson.remember: DPI = sampling density; more is not always necessary.

question: What is a common purpose of a print server?
options: Replace every printer's physical imaging mechanism
Act as an independent substitute for paper and toner
Make every client use the same display driver
Manage and share printer access or print jobs for clients
explanation: A print server centralizes aspects of print access and job management. It does not perform the printer's mechanical imaging stages.

lesson.title: Print server
lesson.meaning: Clients can submit through a shared service rather than manage every connection independently.
lesson.example: An office administers a shared queue through a print server.
lesson.remember: Print server = shared print service and management.

question: During laser printing, what happens in the developing stage?
options: The fuser bonds toner to paper before an image is formed
The finished page is only placed in the output tray
Toner is attracted to the latent image on the photosensitive drum
The paper is scanned into a digital document
explanation: Development places toner onto the electrostatic image. Fusing later bonds toner to the paper through heat and pressure.

lesson.title: Laser development stage
lesson.meaning: Imaging the drum and fixing the paper image are separate stages.
lesson.example: Toner is developed on the drum before transfer to the sheet and final fusing.
lesson.remember: Develop = toner on the image; fuse = bond toner to paper.

question: Which cloud model supplies a managed platform for deploying applications without managing the underlying server OS yourself?
options: SaaS providing only a finished application
PaaS
IaaS requiring the customer to manage the guest OS
A local hypervisor with no managed platform service
explanation: PaaS supplies an application platform while the provider manages underlying platform infrastructure. Responsibilities depend on the service.

lesson.title: PaaS
lesson.meaning: The customer focuses more on application deployment than server administration.
lesson.example: Deploy code to a managed app platform rather than installing the server OS.
lesson.remember: PaaS = platform for applications.

question: Which description best fits a public-cloud service?
options: A provider offers cloud resources to multiple customers under its service model
All customer data must be accessible without authentication
The infrastructure must serve exactly one organization exclusively
Public cloud cannot enforce customer-specific access policies
explanation: Public cloud describes service provision, not automatic public access to all customer data. Access still requires proper controls.

lesson.title: Public cloud
lesson.meaning: Public service availability and public data exposure are different ideas.
lesson.example: A business uses provider-hosted infrastructure with restricted access to its resources.
lesson.remember: Public cloud does not mean all stored data should be public.

question: Which characteristic best identifies a private cloud?
options: Resources necessarily offered to all customers without restriction
Any desktop with a hidden folder
An internet connection that does not use a password
Cloud infrastructure dedicated to one organization
explanation: Private-cloud resources are dedicated to one organization; their location and management arrangement can vary.

lesson.title: Private cloud
lesson.meaning: Dedicated use is the key distinction, not merely a hidden web address.
lesson.example: An organization operates a dedicated cloud environment for its departments.
lesson.remember: Private cloud = dedicated organizational use.

question: What does a hybrid-cloud design combine?
options: Two unconnected USB backup drives
A single desktop running two browser tabs
Distinct cloud environments connected for coordinated use
A switch connected to two identical patch cables
explanation: Hybrid designs integrate distinct environments, commonly private and public clouds, with appropriate connectivity and management.

lesson.title: Hybrid cloud
lesson.meaning: The environments remain distinct while supporting coordinated workloads or data flows.
lesson.example: A business keeps some workloads in a private environment and integrates selected public-cloud services.
lesson.remember: Hybrid = connected use of distinct cloud environments.

question: What does cloud elasticity describe?
options: All provider resources remain permanently fixed despite demand
Adjusting allocated resources as demand changes
Every workload has unlimited free capacity
Adding users automatically eliminates resource limits
explanation: Elastic resources can scale up or down with demand. Configuration, limits and costs still require management.

lesson.title: Elasticity
lesson.meaning: Capacity can follow workload rather than remain fixed.
lesson.example: A service adds capacity for a busy period and reduces it afterward.
lesson.remember: Elasticity = adapt resources to changing demand.

question: What can happen when too many VMs compete for limited host RAM?
options: Host and guest performance can degrade
Every guest automatically receives unlimited physical RAM
Virtual RAM allocations eliminate host memory limits
The storage subsystem permanently becomes main memory
explanation: Virtualization shares finite hardware. Excess allocation or contention can cause paging, slowdowns or failures depending on the platform.

lesson.title: VM resource planning
lesson.meaning: Virtual resources are backed by real limits.
lesson.example: Reduce allocations or add suitable capacity after monitoring host memory pressure.
lesson.remember: Virtualization does not create unlimited host resources.

question: Which setup is an example of a Type 2 hypervisor?
options: A bare-metal hypervisor booted directly on physical hardware
Firmware POST with no guest-management layer
A normal application with no virtualization functions
A desktop virtualization application running within a host OS
explanation: Type 2 virtualization is hosted within an operating-system environment. Type 1 runs directly on the hardware.

lesson.title: Type 2 hypervisor
lesson.meaning: The placement of the virtualization layer defines the distinction.
lesson.example: A learner installs a virtualization application on a normal workstation.
lesson.remember: Type 2 = hosted hypervisor.

question: Which VM network mode typically places a guest on the host's external network as a separate network participant?
options: Disconnected adapter mode
Internal-only networking with no external bridge
Bridged networking
A host-only adapter with no routing to the LAN
explanation: Bridging connects the guest to an external network through the host's networking path. The network's policies still apply.

lesson.title: Bridged VM networking
lesson.meaning: A guest can appear as another device rather than only using a private translated path.
lesson.example: A lab guest obtains an appropriate address on the same external network as permitted.
lesson.remember: Bridged = guest participates on the external network.

question: Which VM mode commonly permits guest outbound connections through the host's NAT engine?
options: A disconnected virtual adapter
NAT networking
A guest with only an isolated internal network and no router
A disk snapshot without a network interface
explanation: NAT translates guest traffic through the host's networking arrangement. Inbound access generally needs additional configuration.

lesson.title: NAT VM networking
lesson.meaning: Outbound convenience does not automatically expose every guest service inbound.
lesson.example: A guest downloads updates through NAT without being directly addressed as an external LAN peer.
lesson.remember: NAT mode commonly supports outbound guest access.

question: Which VM mode is suitable for communication between a host and guests without direct access to the external LAN by that adapter?
options: Host-only networking
Bridged networking onto the external LAN
A guest adapter disconnected from every network
A standard externally bridged virtual NIC by definition
explanation: Host-only networking provides a host/guest network through a virtual interface. Routing or other adapters can change overall connectivity, so inspect the full configuration.

lesson.title: Host-only VM networking
lesson.meaning: A virtual lab can have a private communication segment.
lesson.example: Use host-only mode for a host-to-guest exercise and avoid adding unintended external paths.
lesson.remember: Host-only describes that adapter's network; review all adapters and routing.

question: Why can a conventional 32-bit client OS fail to make all 8 GB of installed RAM usable?
options: All 8 GB automatically becomes CPU cache
A 32-bit application guarantees the whole OS can use all RAM
Memory-generation compatibility becomes irrelevant above 4 GB
Its address-space and platform limits can restrict usable memory
explanation: A 32-bit address space is limited, and platform/OS details affect usable RAM. A compatible 64-bit environment is normally needed to use substantially more memory.

lesson.title: 32-bit addressing
lesson.meaning: Installed capacity and OS-addressable capacity are different.
lesson.example: Check OS architecture and platform support before upgrading a workstation's memory.
lesson.remember: Check hardware and OS memory support, not just the installed total.

question: When installing a 64-bit Windows edition, what driver requirement matters?
options: Any driver with the same product name is compatible
Every 32-bit kernel driver works unchanged on a 64-bit OS
Use supported drivers for that OS and architecture
The device's physical connection removes all architecture requirements
explanation: Drivers interact closely with the OS and hardware. The supported architecture and Windows version must match.

lesson.title: 64-bit drivers
lesson.meaning: Application compatibility does not imply kernel-driver compatibility.
lesson.example: Obtain the vendor's supported 64-bit driver rather than reusing an incompatible older driver.
lesson.remember: Match drivers to the device, OS version and architecture.

question: What is the purpose of Windows activation in a properly licensed installation?
options: Back up user files as part of every activation
Validate the installation's licensing entitlement through the supported process
Automatically test all hardware and device drivers
Create a recovery copy of the previous OS
explanation: Installation and licensing validation are separate aspects of deployment. Activation does not provide backups or guarantee all hardware works.

lesson.title: Activation versus installation
lesson.meaning: A running installer does not settle every licensing requirement.
lesson.example: Use the organization's legitimate licensing and activation procedure.
lesson.remember: Installation, activation and hardware verification are distinct tasks.

question: For a modern UEFI installation using a large disk beyond traditional MBR addressing limits, which partition scheme is normally appropriate?
options: GPT
FAT32 used as a replacement partition table
MBR regardless of its applicable size limits
NTFS used as the firmware boot mode
explanation: GPT is a partitioning scheme suited to modern UEFI deployments and large disks. FAT32 is a file system, not an alternative partition-table scheme.

lesson.title: Large disks
lesson.meaning: Partition layout and file-system format answer different questions.
lesson.example: Plan the supported GPT layout rather than expecting a file-system change alone to solve an MBR limit.
lesson.remember: GPT = partition scheme; NTFS/FAT32 = file systems.

question: What is the primary role of the EFI System Partition in a UEFI OS installation?
options: Store only ordinary user documents
Hold the currently running CPU cache
Replace the need for the OS's bootloader files
Store files used by firmware to boot installed systems
explanation: The EFI System Partition holds boot-related files used in a UEFI environment. Deleting it can prevent startup even when user files remain.

lesson.title: EFI System Partition
lesson.meaning: A disk can contain small system partitions essential to booting.
lesson.example: Do not delete a small unfamiliar boot partition simply to gain space.
lesson.remember: Small system partitions can be critical to startup.

question: Windows setup lists several disks and partitions. What should be done before deleting any partition?
options: Delete every partition because setup lists it
Choose a disk only by its reported size
Identify the correct target and verify authorization and backups
Assume small partitions can never contain critical boot files
explanation: Partition deletion is destructive. Confirm the disk's identity, existing data and recovery arrangements first.

lesson.title: Selecting the target disk
lesson.meaning: Storage operations need exact targets.
lesson.example: Disconnect nonessential drives when appropriate and follow the approved installation plan.
lesson.remember: Verify the target before any delete or format operation.

question: Which choice best describes an in-place OS upgrade compared with a clean installation?
options: It always removes all previous applications by definition
It aims to retain supported applications, settings and data while replacing/upgrading the OS
It eliminates the need for compatibility checks
It is identical to deleting all partitions and starting fresh
explanation: An in-place upgrade aims to preserve supported parts of the existing environment. Compatibility and backup planning remain important.

lesson.title: Upgrade installation
lesson.meaning: Upgrade and fresh installation have different retention goals.
lesson.example: Verify supported upgrade paths and back up before proceeding.
lesson.remember: Upgrade aims to retain; clean install creates a fresh environment.

question: Where should a technician normally obtain a replacement device driver?
options: The device/system vendor or another approved trusted update source
An unsolicited attachment claiming to update all drivers
A package chosen only because its filename matches
An unverified mirror requiring permanent security disabling
explanation: Drivers run with significant system access. Use approved sources and the exact supported device/OS package.

lesson.title: Trusted driver source
lesson.meaning: The origin of system software matters.
lesson.example: Download the supported network driver from the vendor or organization's repository.
lesson.remember: Trusted source + correct model + supported OS.

question: After a basic OS installation succeeds, what should happen before normal deployment?
options: Assume one successful boot proves every device works
Skip required security configuration until a failure occurs
Treat installation completion as a substitute for functional testing
Apply approved updates, verify drivers and test required functions
explanation: A completed installer is only one deployment milestone. Updates, drivers and functional checks prepare the system for actual use.

lesson.title: Post-install updates
lesson.meaning: Ready to boot is not the same as ready for the user's work.
lesson.example: Test networking, display, audio and required applications after approved configuration.
lesson.remember: Install → update/configure → verify → hand over.

question: Which test best verifies the user's actual requirement after a network-adapter driver installation?
options: Only confirm that the installer window closed
Only check that a desktop shortcut exists
Confirm the adapter status and test the required network activity
Assume driver setup proves the required remote service is reachable
explanation: A driver's setup completion does not prove connectivity. Verify the device and the intended network function.

lesson.title: Installation verification
lesson.meaning: Test the outcome the user needs.
lesson.example: Confirm valid configuration and reach the required service after installing the driver.
lesson.remember: Verify function, not just a successful setup message.

question: Which Windows tool is most suitable for reviewing recorded system and application events?
options: Task Manager's live CPU graph
Event Viewer
Disk Management's partition list
Device Manager's hardware tree
explanation: Event Viewer presents event logs that can help correlate failures with time and components. Events require interpretation, not automatic blame.

lesson.title: Event Viewer
lesson.meaning: Logs provide historical evidence.
lesson.example: Review events around an unexpected restart and compare them with the observed symptoms.
lesson.remember: Event Viewer = recorded events, not a live CPU-usage chart.

question: Which Windows management interface can start, stop or configure background services under appropriate authority?
options: Services management console
Task Manager's process list as a substitute for every service setting
Disk Management
The default-program selection panel
explanation: The Services console administers service state and startup behavior. Changes can affect dependencies, so follow the approved procedure.

lesson.title: Services
lesson.meaning: Services perform background functions distinct from interactive applications.
lesson.example: Check an affected service's status and dependencies before restarting it.
lesson.remember: Manage services deliberately; understand dependencies and impact.

question: Why might an approved selective-startup or clean-boot test help diagnose a Windows problem?
options: It permanently repairs every faulty disk
It bypasses the need to verify the affected application
It proves every disabled service is malicious
It can help isolate interference from startup software or services
explanation: Reducing startup components can help isolate software interactions. Follow the documented procedure and restore normal configuration appropriately.

lesson.title: Startup diagnosis
lesson.meaning: An isolation test temporarily changes what starts, not the hardware itself.
lesson.example: A fault disappears under a supported clean-boot test, guiding further startup-component isolation.
lesson.remember: Clean boot is diagnostic isolation, not a universal permanent fix.

question: Which Windows utility shows disks, partitions and volume information?
options: Device Manager's driver tab
Event Viewer's event list
Disk Management
Task Manager's startup list
explanation: Disk Management administers storage layout and volumes. Some operations are destructive and require preparation.

lesson.title: Disk Management
lesson.meaning: Storage structure is separate from the list of running programs.
lesson.example: Inspect a newly attached disk's status before deciding whether initialization is appropriate.
lesson.remember: Inspect first; do not initialize a disk containing needed data by guesswork.

question: What is the main purpose of chkdsk?
options: Validate only protected Windows operating-system file contents
Check a volume's file-system structure and report or repair supported errors with appropriate options
Identify router hops to an internet server
Query DNS server records
explanation: CHKDSK examines a volume and file-system state. Repair options can change data and require suitable backup/recovery planning.

lesson.title: CHKDSK
lesson.meaning: File-system checking is different from checking Windows system-file contents.
lesson.example: Select supported checks after assessing disk health and protecting important data.
lesson.remember: CHKDSK = volume/file-system checks; SFC = protected Windows files.

question: What does DISM commonly help service or repair in Windows administration?
options: Windows images and the component store using supported commands
Physical motherboard socket pins
Printer roller alignment
RAM module notch placement
explanation: DISM is an image-servicing tool. Supported repair workflows can use it to address component-store issues; it is not a hardware repair tool.

lesson.title: DISM
lesson.meaning: Different integrity tools target different system layers.
lesson.example: An administrator follows Microsoft's supported DISM/SFC recovery procedure and reviews results.
lesson.remember: DISM services Windows images/components; use the documented command and source.

question: Why can a process ID (PID) be useful when ending a specific unresponsive process?
options: It supplies the user's authentication password
It identifies a physical network port
It proves a process is safe to terminate without checking
It identifies a particular running process instance
explanation: A PID distinguishes process instances, including cases with similar names. Ending a process can lose unsaved work, so verify the target.

lesson.title: Process ID
lesson.meaning: A name may be shared; an instance identifier is more specific.
lesson.example: Confirm the intended process before using an authorized taskkill operation.
lesson.remember: Verify the process and consequences before ending it.

question: A supported driver update causes a previously working device to fail. Which option may be appropriate after diagnosis?
options: Format all data volumes before assessing the recent change
Keep the failing driver without testing because newer is always better
Roll back to the previous supported driver using the approved process
Replace unrelated network equipment immediately
explanation: A recent driver change can be tested by returning to a known supported version when available. Preserve the ability to recover and verify the result.

lesson.title: Driver rollback
lesson.meaning: Reversing a relevant recent change can test a cause.
lesson.example: Use the supported rollback or reinstall method and retest the device.
lesson.remember: Recent driver change + new fault: investigate and consider supported rollback.

question: A user needs to view a report but must not modify it. Which permission approach follows least privilege?
options: Grant Full Control because Read is always insufficient
Grant appropriate read access without unnecessary write rights
Give local administrator rights for every document
Disable permissions entirely for the containing drive
explanation: Read access meets the stated requirement while unnecessary write or administrative rights increase risk. Effective permissions still depend on the complete policy.

lesson.title: File permissions
lesson.meaning: Permissions should follow the work requirement.
lesson.example: Apply the organization's group-based access process and test the intended read-only behavior.
lesson.remember: Grant the minimum access needed and verify effective access.

question: An approved app needs one documented inbound service port. What is the better firewall change?
options: Add a narrowly scoped approved rule for the required traffic
Disable the firewall on every profile indefinitely
Allow all inbound ports from all sources
Remove the service's authentication requirement
explanation: A specific rule supports the required service while limiting exposure. Broadly disabling protection grants more access than the task needs.

lesson.title: Firewall exception
lesson.meaning: Permit the needed communication, with appropriate scope.
lesson.example: Restrict the rule by port, profile and source where required by policy, then test.
lesson.remember: Narrow, approved exceptions are preferable to disabling the firewall.

question: Which Linux command displays the current working directory?
options: cd
ls
whoami
pwd
explanation: pwd reports the current directory path. It does not change that directory or delete its contents.

lesson.title: pwd
lesson.meaning: A shell operates relative to a current location.
lesson.example: Run pwd before a file operation to confirm where you are.
lesson.remember: pwd = print working directory.

question: Which shell command changes the current working directory?
options: ls
pwd
cd
mkdir
explanation: cd changes the shell's current directory. ls lists entries without changing location.

lesson.title: cd
lesson.meaning: Navigation and listing are separate actions.
lesson.example: Use cd to enter the intended folder, then pwd to verify it.
lesson.remember: cd = change directory; ls = list entries.

question: What is the purpose of chmod on Unix-like systems?
options: Change the file's owner and group by definition
Change file-mode permission bits
List active IP connections
Alter the contents of every matching file
explanation: chmod changes mode permissions for appropriate files. Access and ownership rules still determine who may perform the change.

lesson.title: chmod
lesson.meaning: Permissions govern allowed actions on files and directories.
lesson.example: An authorized administrator grants only the required execute permission to an intended script.
lesson.remember: chmod changes modes; it does not change the file's contents.

question: Which command is commonly used to search text for a matching pattern?
options: grep
mkdir
chown
pwd
explanation: grep searches input text for patterns and prints matching results according to its options. It is useful for examining logs.

lesson.title: grep
lesson.meaning: Filtering text can reveal relevant evidence without changing the source.
lesson.example: Search an approved log for a specific error string.
lesson.remember: grep = text pattern search.

question: In a Unix-like file system, what does a leading slash in /home/user indicate?
options: A relative path under the current folder
A Windows-style drive letter
A network URL that always requires HTTPS
An absolute path beginning at the filesystem root
