explanation: A leading slash starts at the root of the directory hierarchy. Relative paths instead depend on the current directory.

lesson.title: Filesystem root
lesson.meaning: Path meaning depends on where it begins.
lesson.example: /home/user refers to a rooted path regardless of the shell's current folder.
lesson.remember: Leading / = absolute path from filesystem root.

question: Which macOS feature is commonly used for versioned backups and recovery?
options: Disk Utility as a substitute for configured backups
Keychain Access
Time Machine
Activity Monitor
explanation: Time Machine is a macOS backup feature. Its effectiveness depends on configuration, destination availability and recoverability.

lesson.title: Time Machine
lesson.meaning: A recovery feature must be set up before loss occurs.
lesson.example: Verify a Mac's backups and available restore points before major changes.
lesson.remember: Backup configuration and recovery verification still matter.

question: Why should mobile apps normally be installed from trusted, approved sources?
options: It guarantees every app's permissions are necessary
It reduces exposure to untrusted or tampered packages
It removes the need for any further updates
It guarantees the app can never contain a vulnerability
explanation: Trusted distribution reduces risk but does not eliminate it. Review permissions and keep software updated as well.

lesson.title: Application sources
lesson.meaning: App origin is one security layer among several.
lesson.example: Avoid an unsolicited installation package and use the approved distribution path.
lesson.remember: Trusted source, appropriate permissions and updates work together.

question: A mobile app no longer needs location access. What is a suitable action?
options: Revoke that unnecessary permission in the supported settings
Keep the permission forever because it was once approved
Grant unrelated camera and microphone permissions too
Disable all device recovery options instead
explanation: Permissions should reflect current need. Access that once had a purpose can become unnecessary.

lesson.title: Revoking access
lesson.meaning: Least privilege applies over time, not just at installation.
lesson.example: Review app permissions after changing how a device is used.
lesson.remember: Remove access that is no longer required.

question: Before an authorized remote wipe of a lost managed device, what consequence must be considered?
options: It guarantees the device will be physically returned
It is equivalent to displaying the device on a map
It changes only the screen-lock timeout
It can destroy device data and must follow approval and recovery policy
explanation: Remote wipe is destructive. Use the organization's authorization, device-management and recovery procedures rather than treating it as a harmless locator action.

lesson.title: Remote wipe
lesson.meaning: Locating, locking and wiping have different consequences.
lesson.example: An authorized team verifies the target and backup requirements before executing a wipe.
lesson.remember: Wipe can erase data; target and approval matter.

question: Before resetting a phone for troubleshooting, what should be verified?
options: Assume all local app data survives every reset
Reset first and investigate account recovery afterward
Required data backup, account/recovery access and authorization
Treat a reset as a harmless display-setting change
explanation: A reset can remove local data and settings and trigger account verification requirements. Plan recovery before resetting.

lesson.title: Factory reset preparation
lesson.meaning: Reset is a change with data and access consequences.
lesson.example: Confirm important data and account recovery arrangements before following the approved reset procedure.
lesson.remember: Protect data and recovery access before resetting.

question: Which malware description best fits a Trojan horse?
options: Malware defined primarily by self-propagation across systems
Malicious software presented as something legitimate or useful
A cryptographic integrity checksum
A legitimate signed program with no malicious behavior
explanation: A Trojan relies on deceptive appearance or purpose to get executed. It need not replicate like a worm.

lesson.title: Trojan horse
lesson.meaning: The disguise encourages the user to trust the program.
lesson.example: An unofficial 'utility' installs unwanted remote access instead of doing only what it promises.
lesson.remember: Trojan = deceptive legitimate-looking software with malicious behavior.

question: What distinguishes a computer worm from a simple non-replicating malicious program?
options: It can self-propagate across systems under suitable conditions
It is defined solely by pretending to be a useful app
It cannot move between systems under any conditions
It is simply every unwanted browser setting
explanation: Worms can spread copies through available pathways or vulnerabilities. This differs from merely disguising one executable as useful.

lesson.title: Worm
lesson.meaning: Propagation is the defining distinction in this question.
lesson.example: An unpatched network service enables a worm to spread between vulnerable machines.
lesson.remember: Worm = self-propagating malware.

question: A workstation is suspected of active ransomware. What is an appropriate initial organizational response?
options: Attach all writable backup disks to the affected PC
Erase every relevant log before notifying anyone
Continue normal file sharing regardless of the incident plan
Follow the incident plan and contain/isolate the affected system as directed
explanation: Containment can limit spread and further harm. Follow the incident plan, preserve required evidence and use approved recovery processes.

lesson.title: Ransomware response
lesson.meaning: Active compromise needs coordinated incident handling.
lesson.example: Notify the responsible team and isolate network access as instructed.
lesson.remember: Contain, report and follow the incident plan; protect recovery copies.

question: An unknown person follows an employee through a secured door without presenting authorization. What is this commonly called?
options: Phishing
Shoulder surfing
Tailgating
Disk imaging
explanation: Tailgating bypasses physical access procedures by following someone else. Respond through the organization's safety and access-control process.

lesson.title: Tailgating
lesson.meaning: Physical entry can undermine digital controls.
lesson.example: An employee uses the approved visitor-verification process instead of assuming the follower is authorized.
lesson.remember: Tailgating = unauthorized entry by following an authorized person.

question: Which action is an example of shoulder surfing?
options: A deceptive email requesting credentials
Watching someone enter a password or view sensitive data
Following someone through an access-controlled door
Encrypting files for approved storage
explanation: Shoulder surfing obtains information by observation. Screens, keyboards and surroundings can expose secrets.

lesson.title: Shoulder surfing
lesson.meaning: Information can leak without malware.
lesson.example: Position a screen appropriately and avoid entering sensitive information while someone can observe it.
lesson.remember: Shoulder surfing = observing sensitive information directly.

question: What should a user do before leaving an authenticated workstation unattended?
options: Lock the session according to policy
Leave the authenticated session available to passersby
Share the password so colleagues can unlock it
Rely only on the monitor entering power-saving mode
explanation: Locking restricts casual access to an already authenticated session. It complements other controls rather than replacing them.

lesson.title: Unattended workstation
lesson.meaning: A strong login is ineffective if an unlocked session is left available.
lesson.example: Lock the workstation before stepping away even for a short period.
lesson.remember: Authenticated does not mean safe to leave unlocked.

question: Which statement best distinguishes hashing from encryption?
options: A cryptographic hash normally contains a decryptable copy of the original
Encryption is designed to be irreversible even with the correct key
Both are identical lossless compression operations
Hashing produces a digest for uses such as integrity checking; encryption is designed for recovery with the correct key
explanation: Cryptographic hashes and encryption serve different purposes. A digest can support integrity verification, while encryption protects recoverable data confidentiality.

lesson.title: Hashing versus encryption
lesson.meaning: One operation summarizes data; the other transforms it for controlled recovery.
lesson.example: Compare an official download digest to detect a mismatch rather than expecting the digest to contain a decryptable copy.
lesson.remember: Hash = digest. Encryption = reversible with the appropriate key.

question: Which distinction is correct?
options: A firewall is a replacement for every antimalware measure
Antimalware replaces all traffic-filtering policies
A firewall controls traffic by rules; antimalware tools detect or respond to malicious software
Both controls exclusively address physical theft
explanation: These controls address different parts of security. Neither substitutes for every other layer.

lesson.title: Firewall versus antivirus
lesson.meaning: Layered protection uses tools with different functions.
lesson.example: A host uses appropriate traffic rules, antimalware controls, updates and limited privileges.
lesson.remember: Traffic control and malware detection are different roles.

question: Which measure directly helps prevent unauthorized physical removal of a workstation?
options: Changing only the operating-system wallpaper
Appropriate physical access controls and securing equipment
Renaming the device on the network
Increasing the monitor's auto-off delay
explanation: Physical controls address access to and removal of equipment. Software settings alone do not prevent someone carrying away an unsecured device.

lesson.title: Physical security
lesson.meaning: Protect the hardware as well as its data.
lesson.example: Use controlled rooms or appropriate equipment locks according to policy.
lesson.remember: Physical access is part of information security.

question: What is the purpose of keeping multiple backup copies on different media or locations, including an off-site copy?
options: Reduce dependence on one device, location or failure event
Guarantee recovery without ever testing a backup
Replace every access-control requirement
Keep all copies permanently writable from the same compromised account
explanation: Diverse protected copies reduce shared failure exposure. Recovery testing and security remain necessary.

lesson.title: Backup diversity
lesson.meaning: One event should not destroy the working data and every recovery copy.
lesson.example: A site incident destroys local equipment while a protected off-site backup remains available.
lesson.remember: Separate failure domains and test recovery.

question: Which opening question best invites a user to describe a problem without prematurely narrowing the cause?
options: Your RAM is broken, right?
You must have deleted Windows, correct?
The fault is definitely the keyboard, isn't it?
What happens when you try to open the application?
explanation: An open question gathers the user's account before suggesting a diagnosis. Leading questions can distort useful information.

lesson.title: Open questions
lesson.meaning: Start broad, then narrow with focused follow-up questions.
lesson.example: Ask what happens, when it started and whether anything changed.
lesson.remember: Open questions gather context; closed questions confirm details.

question: What does a support service-level agreement normally define?
options: A guarantee that every system will be fault-free forever
A list of all customers' private credentials
Agreed service commitments such as response targets and scope
Only a hardware manufacturer's CPU socket diagram
explanation: An SLA documents agreed service expectations. It is not a promise that faults are impossible.

lesson.title: SLA
lesson.meaning: Support priorities should follow agreed commitments and impact.
lesson.example: A ticket is prioritized using the applicable response target and severity policy.
lesson.remember: SLA = agreed service expectations, not zero risk.

question: Why is a chain-of-custody record important when handling potential digital evidence?
options: Increase the storage device's physical speed
It documents who handled evidence and when, supporting traceability
Replace every evidence-integrity procedure
Permit unrecorded transfers whenever the technician is experienced
explanation: Evidence handling must preserve required integrity and traceability. Record transfers and follow the approved process.

lesson.title: Chain of custody
lesson.meaning: An unexplained handover can undermine confidence in evidence handling.
lesson.example: Log an evidence transfer with the required identifiers, time and responsible parties.
lesson.remember: Record possession and transfers; preserve integrity under the approved process.

question: Before starting an authorized remote-support session on a customer's PC, what should be confirmed?
options: The customer's consent, intended scope and approved access procedure
Assume permission for support allows access to unrelated files
Skip user identity and device checks entirely
Treat every remote session as authorized without consent
explanation: Remote access can expose user data and control. Confirm permission, identity and scope under the support procedure.

lesson.title: Remote support consent
lesson.meaning: Access for support is limited to the agreed work.
lesson.example: Explain the intended remote actions and obtain the required consent before connecting.
lesson.remember: Confirm consent and scope; use approved remote-support tools.

question: What is an appropriate approach when a support task needs the user to authenticate?
options: Store the password in a public support-ticket field
Copy it into unrelated diagnostic logs
Reuse it on a personal technician account
Have the user authenticate through the approved process without unnecessarily disclosing their password
explanation: Support should avoid unnecessary collection and exposure of secrets. Use the approved identity and authentication workflow.

lesson.title: Credential handling
lesson.meaning: Solving the fault does not justify unrestricted handling of credentials.
lesson.example: The user enters credentials privately when required by the authorized procedure.
lesson.remember: Minimize exposure of secrets; follow the approved authentication process.

question: Why should a significant approved change include a rollback plan?
options: Avoid every post-change verification step
Guarantee a backup is no longer required
To provide a defined recovery path if the change fails
Conceal the change from the affected support team
explanation: A rollback plan identifies how to return to a known acceptable state, subject to the change's capabilities and data effects.

lesson.title: Rollback planning
lesson.meaning: Plan for failure before making the change.
lesson.example: Record recovery steps and required backups before a configuration deployment.
lesson.remember: Change plan = intended action, validation and recovery path.

question: A customer requests installation of software without an appropriate license. What should the technician do?
options: Use an unapproved activation bypass
Follow licensing policy and use legitimate authorized options
Copy an unrelated customer's entitlement
Assume downloading proves permission for every use
explanation: Technical ability to install does not establish permission to use software. Follow the applicable license and organizational process.

lesson.title: Software licensing
lesson.meaning: Deployment includes authorization as well as technical setup.
lesson.example: Offer an approved licensed product or legitimate alternative.
lesson.remember: A download is not proof of a valid license for the intended use.

question: Before retiring a storage device with sensitive organizational data, what is required?
options: An approved sanitization or destruction method appropriate to the device and policy
Only delete shortcuts to the sensitive files
Only rename the stored documents
Assume emptying the recycle bin always meets sanitization requirements
explanation: Ordinary deletion does not guarantee suitable sanitization. Methods depend on the storage technology and organizational requirements.

lesson.title: Data sanitization
lesson.meaning: Retiring hardware includes protecting the information it held.
lesson.example: Use the approved verified process before reuse or disposal.
lesson.remember: Deletion and approved sanitization are not equivalent.

question: A frustrated customer describes repeated failures. Which response is most professional?
options: Dismiss the report before gathering evidence
Use technical jargon to prevent follow-up questions
Blame the customer as the initial diagnosis
Acknowledge the impact, clarify the symptoms and explain the next steps calmly
explanation: Professional support combines respectful communication with evidence-based diagnosis. Dismissing the user harms understanding and trust.

lesson.title: Empathy in support
lesson.meaning: Empathy helps keep the conversation useful and focused.
lesson.example: Confirm how the fault affects the user, then gather details and set realistic expectations.
lesson.remember: Acknowledge impact, clarify facts and communicate next steps.

question: Which information best supports an escalation to another technical team?
options: Only an unsupported conclusion with no test results
Only the message still broken
Symptoms, impact, relevant logs, tests already tried and their results
All unrelated personal files regardless of need
explanation: An effective handover gives the receiving team enough context to continue without repeating work or relying on assumptions.

lesson.title: Useful escalation
lesson.meaning: Escalation transfers evidence and responsibility through the approved process.
lesson.example: Attach relevant error details and test outcomes while minimizing unnecessary personal data.
lesson.remember: Escalate facts, impact and attempted actions.
